rv.q: It’s an honest effort to explore why some people just keep wanting more stuff, which most of us of a certain age learn is clearly pointless, while also admiring the force of personality it takes to procure them.
And Chenoweth is a wonder, sounding a little bit country whenever Jackie is most herself

Chenoweth, who was born to be in a spangly dress and center stage on Broadway, is perfect for the role, an always-welcome jolt of in-on-it theatricality, but is let down by dialogue that’s not as funny as it could be and with a character too unfocused.
She never looks less than perfectly photoshopped, but the production ultimately overtaxes her strengths.
But you can forgive us for not caring.

More’s the pity, then, that the musical “The Queen of Versailles” proves to be so unwieldy and uninspired: awkwardly constructed, with a plodding book by Lindsey Ferrentino and a score by Mr. Schwartz that gives little scope for its star’s prodigious vocal gifts.
Rather than decide whether to romanticize or satirize its subjects, the musical ventures a gaudy and confused mix of both without a coherent point of view.
Like the rest of the show, however, the score doesn’t quite cohere; it feels like less than the sum of its parts.
Unfortunately, Greenfield’s dazzling assessment of greed, consumption and the American dream doesn’t translate on the stage.
Or you could save the money and have someone slap you back and forth with a large salmon.

It is the confused, contorted product of a set of absolutely incompatible impulses: to ogle, even lionize the Über-rich but also to critique them; to revel in conspicuous consumption and also to satirize it.
The Orlando-area colossus comes to represent the criminally bad show it’s in — a wrecking ball to good taste that opened Sunday night at the St. James Theatre.
This lavishly overstuffed, irresistibly entertaining confection is impossible to imagine without her.

Or maybe they had fallen in love with Kristin Chenoweth, who exudes such charm and charisma that even Jackie’s most appalling statements of white privilege and unbridled capitalism lose some of their shocking edge.

The Queen of Versailles may have opened on Broadway with its scaffolding still up, but it’s still compellingly ambitious in its scope and bold in its merciless portrayal of its greed-enflamed protagonist, who fiercely battles her own burgeoning self-awareness.
The Queen of Versailles is too much a creature of excess to ever comment seriously on it.
But it doesn’t adequately answer for me Sondheim’s essential question: Why should this be a musical?
So, spending nearly 3 hours with her and her billionaire timeshare-tycoon husband, David (F. Murray Abraham), in this busy but only fitfully engaging new Broadway musical is a long sit.

In a year when Broadway has given us genuinely ambitious work grappling with what it means to be American, "The Queen of Versailles" offers only spectacle without insight, a palace with no one home. What were they thinking?
On the whole, Queen the musical has been shot through a vaselined lens.
Now, that intriguing late turn hardly redeems the plodding narrative that has preceded it.
On the other hand, if you are looking for a a story line that engages and excites you, well, that is not happening here.

The insurmountable problem with The Queen of Versailles is that we are given no reason to care one way or the other about this spendthrift family, not even when they nearly lose their property during the 2008 financial crisis.
By the act-ending moment when Chenoweth is downstage center declaring with 'This is Not the Way' that the 2008 financial crash that bankrupted David won't stop her, only boredom has set in.
In the end, “The Queen of Versailles” really is the only show on Broadway that has everything but Yul Brynner – and it firmly remains a puzzlement!
It’s neither a credible hero’s journey nor a compelling antihero’s one; it’s simply soulless, requiring The Queen of Versailles to steal a soul for its storytelling stakes.
The palatial final vista feels as cold and empty, and as cheap-feeling and gaudily underwhelming, as the show itself
The frivolous first act and the stirring second act deliciously dance together.

But the arguably unfixable problem of The Queen of Versailles is a heroine who gives away her secrets in the first scene, leaving her insufficiently interesting to carry a two-act musical, especially one so unsure about what it wants to say.

Without moral perspective, without characters who earn our emotional investment, without formal innovation that justifies broken conventions, the evening just sits there—expensive, elaborately designed, professionally performed, utterly beside the point.
Even Kristin Chenoweth’s desperate charm can’t salvage this cringy musical about building America’s largest home—a Broadway construction site that never finds its foundation.
This ill-timed trudge of a show seems content to watch her eat cake — with a supersize side of McDonald's fries.

cn.t: Critics are sharply divided on this Stephen Schwartz-Kristin Chenoweth musical about American excess, with most finding it tonally confused and unable to decide whether to satirize or celebrate its billionaire subject, though Chenoweth's performance earns widespread praise.

sg.ra: TickPick and Headout both name Center Orchestra rows E-J (TickPick: E-J; SeatPlan/Headout: F-O) as the prime zone at the Barrymore because the 1,058-seat house is shallow enough that the mezzanine overhang only kicks in at row K of the orchestra, leaving center rows F-J with an uncovered, forward sightline well-suited to the text-driven plays this house tends to book.

Headout and TickPick both warn against Orchestra rows A-C at the Barrymore specifically because the stage at this 1928 house sits high relative to the front rows — TickPick: 'rows A, B, and C are too close to the stage and might block your view'; Headout adds that 'seats closer to the stage may cause neck strain from looking upward.'

SeatPlan and TickPick both confirm the Barrymore mezzanine overhang begins at row K of the orchestra but isn't obstructive — SeatPlan: 'those sitting in the rear of the Orchestra section will notice that the stage feels impressively close'; the house's well-raked orchestra keeps sightlines intact even under cover, which matters because this is a 1,058-seat intimate-play house and losing the rear orchestra would shrink the good-seat pool significantly.

sg.vl: Elevated wide view, under premium pricing
sg.ra: SeatPlan directly names row A Center Front Mezzanine as the house favorite at the Barrymore — 'very popular thanks to its fantastic elevated position above the stage' — and both SeatPlan and TickPick emphasize the Barrymore's front mezzanine is only 5 rows deep (A-E, 196 seats), so even row E retains a wide, pitched view and benefits from the intimate 1,058-seat scale.

SeatPlan specifically praises the Barrymore rear mezzanine rake: 'a decent rake means even the back rows offer a surprisingly good look at the stage' and 'even in the far corner theatergoers won't feel too much strain to make out the stage.' The house's three-flights-up rear mezz is the trade-off for the small footprint, but the rake compensates for distance in a way deeper houses don't manage.

Headout and TickPick both flag the Barrymore's six box seats (three per side of the orchestra) and the orchestra rows D-E directly beneath them as compromised — Headout: 'seats under the Boxes in rows D and E a little restricted'; TickPick adds 'far Left and Right Orchestra and the outer corners of the Mezzanine can have reduced sightlines.' This is a specific quirk of the Barrymore's 1928 proscenium layout with built-in side boxes.
